fixes.explanation: Compassion, friend. Isaiah says, “For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob…” before anything else happens. The very first thing Jacob gets is the LORD's tenderness. Then the verse says He will once again choose Israel and settle them in their own land.

I get why you'd guess that, since this song gets sharp later on. But verse 1 starts softer. Isaiah says the LORD will have compassion on Jacob. And Jacob gets a homeland, because the LORD will settle them in their own land.
Sending them away sounds like a clean ending, but that's not what the verse says. Isaiah says Israel “…will make captives of their captors…” The captors are the ones made captive.

Mourning is a decent guess, because a king falling feels like something people might grieve. But Isaiah says people will sing “…this song of contempt against the king of Babylon…” It's sung against the king, not for him.
Pharaoh is a name people know, so it's an easy one to grab. But he isn't in this song. The song says, “The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked…” Look to the LORD for this one.
I see why prophets came to mind. But the verse names a different group. Sheol stirs up the spirits of the dead, and they are all the rulers of the earth. The prophets aren't mentioned here.

A ruler taking over sounds like how a king might think. But the kings in Sheol don't hand him anything. They say, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” They call him weak, just like them.
I bet that's a welcome he'd have wanted. But the dead kings tell him, “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” Strong is the last word they use. They call him weak.

Defender would be a kinder title. But the song says, “You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations.” Defender isn't the title the song gives him. It calls him a “…destroyer of nations.”
That's the last "I will." He says, “I will make myself like the Most High.” The Most High is God. Then the song says he will be brought down to Sheol (Isaiah 14:15).

Building a temple would be a humble plan. But his last words are, “I will make myself like the Most High.” Building something for the LORD isn't what he says. He says he will make himself like the Most High.

Valley of Hinnom is a specific place name, but this song never mentions it. The song says, “But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit.” That's where he ends up. He was aiming up, and the song says down.
That's the question. Those who see him ask, “Is this the man who shook the earth…” I bet they can hardly believe it's the same guy. He made kingdoms tremble, and now people just stare.

That's the reason the song gives. “You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people.” Burial with the other kings is what he doesn't get. The reason is what he did to his own land and people.
A missing tomb would be a simple reason. But the song gives a different one: “…since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people.” That names why. A tomb isn't the point.
That's an easy thing to imagine, but the song never says it. It gives this reason: “…since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people.” His sons aren't named as the reason.

I can see why you'd think that, but it's the opposite. The song says, “They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities.” So the sons don't get to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities.

False is right. The song says, “They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities.” The text says "never," so they don't get to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities.
Broom, friend. The LORD says, “I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction…” The tool is a broom, and the word that goes with it is destruction. That word "sweep" gives it away.
